title: Adult surgical wounds that heal by regeneration rather than fibrosis

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an intervention applied during surgery that enables adult wounds to restore tissue architecture and function while closing safely and on time. Its intended scope includes skin, bowel, peritoneum and tendon. Success would mean rebuilding the structures that give each tissue its function, rather than merely reducing the amount or visibility of scar. The intervention remains hypothetical in the supplied evidence.

Early fetal skin healing provides a biological precedent for repair with little scarring and restoration of structures such as skin appendages. The supplied research describes a transition toward scarring in human fetal skin around 22–24 weeks. That timing was attributed to indexed introductory text examined in an earlier research pass; no retained source text is available in this record to verify it. Fetal healing motivates the proposal, but does not establish that a single developmental program can be switched back on across several adult surgical tissues.

Reducing fibrosis or preventing postoperative adhesions could contribute to this capability, but neither outcome alone demonstrates regeneration. Adhesion prevention concerns unwanted attachments between surfaces; regenerative repair also requires restoration of the injured tissue itself. The supplied anti-JUN study addresses the adhesion component, without establishing the broader multi-tissue capability.

significance.text: If achieved, regenerative surgical repair would change the expected outcome of tissue injury: a safely closed wound could recover its original organization and mechanical function, including structures that ordinary scar repair does not reliably restore. The proposed direct outcomes include skin with recovered dermal architecture and appendages, bowel anastomoses without clinically important narrowing, peritoneal surfaces that heal without adhesions, and tendons with restored organization and load-bearing function. These are intended outcomes, not demonstrated achievements.

The clinical importance extends beyond the appearance of a scar. Fibrotic repair can contract tissue, narrow hollow organs, restrict the movement of tendons or nerves, and create attachments within the abdomen. The supplied adhesion research identifies postoperative adhesions as a substantial surgical problem. A treatment that durably prevented them could reduce adhesion-related complications, but fewer adhesions in an experimental model would not by itself establish reductions in bowel obstruction, pain or the difficulty of later surgery; those benefits require clinical outcome evidence.

The impact depends on achieving several properties together. Less fibrosis could be valuable without restoring native architecture, while a wound that appears regenerated could still have inadequate strength or develop a late stricture. The premise therefore should not be expressed as a claim that every adult incision, anastomosis or serosal injury necessarily heals by scar. The relevant target is harmful fibrotic repair in defined wounds and tissues, with functional recovery demonstrated directly.

Regenerating a wound also has a narrower meaning than replacing a missing limb, complex body part or solid organ. Repair within an existing tissue does not establish the ability to generate the larger geometry, coordinated tissue types and connections required for a missing replacement. Such replacement could benefit from regenerative wound integration, but would require additional capabilities.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is controllable regeneration in adult surgical wounds without sacrificing reliable closure. Describing this as a single switch is a mechanistic hypothesis, not an established discovery. The intervention would need to coordinate repair sufficiently to restore tissue-specific architecture while retaining the early mechanical integrity needed to prevent wound separation or anastomotic leakage. A common intervention across tissues is an ambitious proposed requirement; the supplied materials do not establish a shared mechanism that would make it possible.

The fetal-skin analogy leaves a major translation problem. The cited review concerns extracellular matrix components and regulators associated with scarless fetal healing, whereas the proposed treatment must work in adult tissue after an operation. The supplied evidence does not establish which features of fetal repair are necessary or sufficient, how to reproduce them controllably in adults, or whether mechanisms relevant to skin would also regenerate bowel, peritoneum and tendon.

Proposed engineering barriers include delivering the intervention to the relevant wound compartments, controlling its duration and local activity, and balancing reduced pathological matrix deposition against sufficient structural repair. Each tissue presents a different reconstruction target: dermis and appendages in skin, organized bowel wall, a restored mesothelial surface in the peritoneum, and aligned load-bearing structures in tendon. Demonstrating reduced fibrosis or preserved burst strength alone would leave these architectural questions unanswered.

The reported sustained-release anti-JUN hydrogel illustrates a narrower approach to local control of postoperative fibrosis and adhesions. Even if its reported animal results are confirmed, the remaining breakthrough is to connect such control to genuine tissue reconstruction and durable function across the proposed wound types. Adhesion suppression cannot be used as a substitute for evidence of skin regeneration, bowel-wall restoration or tendon recovery.

current_state.text: The supplied bibliography identifies Gomes and colleagues’ review, Fetal skin wound healing: key extracellular matrix components and regulators in scarless healing, as published online on August 16, 2024, and assigned to the February 2025 issue of the Journal of Investigative Dermatology, volume 145, pages 280–302. These are two publication dates in the supplied metadata; calling it a 2025 review is consistent with its listed issue year. The publication history was not independently verified in the supplied review.

The research attributes to that review the general observation that deeper adult skin wounds usually scar, in contrast to early fetal skin healing with restoration of appendages. It further reports scarless human fetal healing until approximately week 22 and adult-like histology after week 24. These details should remain attributed and qualified: the publisher page reportedly did not load during direct retrieval, the earlier pass reportedly used an institutional PDF and indexed text, and neither the source text nor an artifact hash was retained for the supplied evidence review. The record therefore preserves the reported timing without treating it as independently verified here or as a universal developmental cutoff.

The second supplied paper is Foster and colleagues’ Postoperative adhesions are abrogated by a sustained-release anti-JUN therapeutic in preclinical models, published in Science Translational Medicine on March 12, 2025, volume 17, article eadp9957. The reconciled research reports that a sustained-release JUN inhibitor delivered in a hydrogel reduced adhesion quantity and fibrosis in mice and pigs after abdominal surgery, including a bowel-resection model. This is a reported preclinical adhesion result, not a human demonstration of regenerative surgical healing.

The supplied abstract excerpt reports adhesion prevention without deleterious effects on bowel anastomosis or abdominal-wall healing. That supports an attributed account of the authors’ healing observations, but does not establish comprehensive safety, native bowel burst strength, freedom from later stricture or restoration of normal tissue architecture. No retained article text, methods, numerical effect sizes, follow-up details or artifact hashes were available to the supplied review, so those aspects cannot be assessed from this record.

The same supplied abstract places adhesion formation after 50–90% of abdominal operations and characterizes prevention and treatment as lacking a proven strategy. That range and characterization are the authors’ reported clinical context, not a newly verified estimate or an assessment of every available intervention. The research also describes physical barriers as clinical tools with limited effect, but the supplied review could not verify their comparative efficacy. These materials do not establish current clinical practice or the field’s completeness as of November 1, 2026.

Taken together, the supplied materials describe a fetal-skin biological precedent and a narrower preclinical anti-adhesion approach. They do not establish achievement of the proposed multi-tissue regenerative intervention. The missing retained documents limit verification of the historical reports; that limitation is not evidence that the reported results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: apply one defined intervention during surgery, first in adult large animals and subsequently in appropriately designed human studies, using prespecified efficacy and safety criteria. Define dose, delivery, timing, wound models, comparators and measurement methods in advance. Early wound strength must be sufficient for safe closure, with direct assessment of wound separation, anastomotic leakage and other relevant healing complications. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Defined intervention enables safe closure in adult animals and humans

completion_criteria.text: For skin, a full-thickness wound should restore dermal architecture and epidermal appendages, together with quantitatively assessed mechanical recovery. Histological and functional measurements should distinguish regeneration from a thinner, softer or less visible scar. Appendage recovery should be evaluated against appropriate uninjured tissue, with the structures and extent of recovery specified before the study.
completion_criteria.label: Full-thickness skin wounds restore architecture, appendages and mechanical function

completion_criteria.text: For bowel, an anastomosis should restore tissue architecture, avoid clinically important stricture and recover burst strength comparable to matched uninjured bowel at prespecified time points. The comparison should account for anatomical site and measurement method. Early safety and later lumen caliber should both be assessed, because adequate burst strength alone does not demonstrate regeneration or exclude narrowing.
completion_criteria.label: Bowel architecture and burst strength match uninjured bowel without clinically important stricture

completion_criteria.text: For peritoneum, a standardized injury should restore the mesothelial surface and show no adhesions at a prespecified re-look beyond 90 days. The injury model, adhesion assessment and observation period should be defined in advance. Absence of adhesions is a relevant outcome, but evidence of surface restoration is also needed to support a regenerative interpretation. A later clinical claim of fewer adhesive obstructions would require separate outcome evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Peritoneal mesothelium restored without adhesions at re-look beyond 90 days

completion_criteria.text: Because the intended scope includes tendon, an additional proposed criterion is required: restoration of tendon architecture, mechanical performance and gliding function without clinically important tethering. Its injury model, comparator and acceptable functional thresholds remain to be specified. Passing only the skin, bowel and peritoneal tests would demonstrate a narrower scope than the full concept.
completion_criteria.label: Tendon architecture, mechanics and gliding recover without clinically important tethering

completion_criteria.text: Convincing evidence should include reproducibility across independent teams, blinded outcome assessment where feasible and sufficiently long follow-up to detect late fibrosis, strictures or loss of function. Results should state the tested tissues, wound sizes, anatomical sites and patient or animal conditions. A finite set of successful tests establishes demonstrated breadth within those boundaries; it does not establish literal universality across adult surgical wounds.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce results with long-term follow-up and stated limits

related_concepts.text: SUR-09, Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply, and SUR-12, Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation, overlap through regenerative biology and the need for functional tissue integration. SUR-05 concerns healing an existing surgical wound. Creating a replacement part or organ additionally requires its larger architecture, perfusion and coordinated connections. Successful wound regeneration could assist implantation without satisfying either replacement concept.

SUR-04, Restoration of volitional function after complete spinal cord transection, shares the concern that tissue repair must recover function rather than merely close an injury. Its defining outcome requires neural continuity and useful control of movement. A wound with less fibrosis or restored local architecture would not by itself demonstrate those capabilities.

SUR-07, Incisionless resection and reconstruction inside the closed body, could benefit from regenerative healing at internal reconstruction sites. Its defining advance is access and operative reconstruction without an external incision; SUR-05 concerns the biological outcome of injured tissue regardless of how the operation reaches it.

SUR-10, Cell-identity-selective extirpation inside an organ that keeps working, and SUR-11, Real-time cellular and molecular vision of the intact operative field, could respectively reduce collateral injury or help measure tissue responses. Selective removal and operative sensing remain distinct from inducing regeneration, and neither would alone meet SUR-05’s architectural, mechanical and healing criteria.

change_log.change: Replaced the universal claim that every adult surgical injury heals by scar with a tissue- and wound-dependent description of harmful fibrotic repair.
change_log.reason: The original statement exceeded the supplied evidence and obscured differences among injury types.

change_log.change: Preserved the intervention’s cross-tissue ambition while treating a single regenerative switch as a hypothesis.
change_log.reason: The supplied materials do not establish a shared fetal program that can be restored across adult skin, bowel, peritoneum and tendon.

change_log.change: Retained the approximately 22–24-week fetal transition as an attributed, qualified report.
change_log.reason: The quantitative detail is useful, but its supporting text was not retained for verification; missing evidence does not establish that the timing is false.

change_log.change: Integrated the supplied online publication date and journal issue date for the fetal-skin review.
change_log.reason: The supplied metadata distinguishes August 2024 online publication from February 2025 issue assignment. This accounts for the two year labels without claiming independent verification.

change_log.change: Preserved the reported anti-JUN animal models, bowel-resection context, healing observations and 50–90% adhesion range with explicit attribution and access limitations.
change_log.reason: These details explain the reported advance, while the absence of retained methods and source artifacts limits assessment of efficacy, safety and generalizability.

change_log.change: Separated adhesion prevention, tissue regeneration, mechanical recovery and downstream clinical benefit.
change_log.reason: Each is a distinct outcome; success on one does not establish the others.

change_log.change: Added architectural measures, matched bowel-strength comparisons, prespecified safety endpoints and a proposed tendon criterion.
change_log.reason: The original functional tests did not fully demonstrate regeneration and omitted one tissue in the intended scope.

change_log.change: Added reproducibility, follow-up and explicit boundaries to the proposed demonstrations.
change_log.reason: Finite testing can establish a convincing range of performance without proving universal effectiveness.

change_log.change: Expanded roster relationships while preserving each concept’s separate identity.
change_log.reason: Regenerative wound healing may support replacement, neural repair, internal reconstruction and operative sensing, but does not establish those capabilities.

unresolved_issues: Neither source has retained text or artifact hashes in the supplied source index. The precise fetal timing and the anti-JUN study’s methods, efficacy, follow-up and safety observations remain unverified within this record.
The supplied metadata explains the fetal review’s 2024 online and 2025 issue labels, but its publication history has not been independently checked.
No supplied evidence establishes whether one intervention can regenerate all four intended tissues or whether tissue-specific treatments would be necessary.
Operational thresholds for early wound strength, architectural recovery, bowel comparability, clinically important stricture and tendon function remain to be defined.
The comparative effectiveness of existing adhesion barriers and other preventive approaches, and the field’s status as of November 1, 2026, are not established by the supplied materials.

The review’s suggestion to reduce current-state reporting largely to bibliographic identification was not adopted in full. Attributed historical details were retained to preserve useful research content, with verification limits stated explicitly.

brief.title: Surgical wounds that rebuild working tissue
possible: After surgery, a wound could close safely and on time while rebuilding the tissue’s original structure and function. A treatment applied during the operation would help adult skin, bowel, the abdominal lining and tendons heal this way.

Skin could recover its normal layers and structures such as hair follicles. Joined bowel could heal without harmful narrowing, abdominal surfaces without unwanted attachments, and tendons with restored strength and movement.
why: Scar tissue can shrink, narrow organs and restrict movement. Restoring working tissue would change recovery for surgical patients in ways that go beyond how a scar looks.

sources.showed: This review examines the material surrounding cells and the regulators involved in fetal skin healing without scars.
sources.cited_for: Early fetal skin healing provides a biological precedent for restoring tissue structures with little scarring.
sources.not_established: Fetal healing does not establish a treatment that can rebuild adult surgical wounds across different tissues.

sources.showed: This animal study tests a slowly released drug that blocks JUN, a regulator involved in unwanted tissue attachments after surgery.
sources.cited_for: The study supports a narrower approach to reducing unwanted attachments and scar tissue after abdominal surgery.
sources.not_established: Preventing attachments does not establish restored tissue architecture, durable function or safety in humans.

shown: Foster and colleagues reported fewer adhesions—unwanted attachments between tissue surfaces—and less scar tissue in mice and pigs after abdominal surgery. They reported no harmful effects on healing of joined bowel or the abdominal wall. This was an animal result.
missing: A treatment that rebuilds adult tissue while preserving the early strength needed to prevent wounds reopening or joined bowel leaking.
Direct evidence that skin, bowel, the abdominal lining and tendons recover their normal structures and function.
Reliable local delivery with control over how long the treatment acts.
Independent confirmation and long follow-up showing that recovery lasts without late narrowing or loss of function.

milestones.label: A defined treatment permits safe closure in animals and humans
milestones.explanation: The same defined treatment would have to support safe closure first in adult large animals, then in human studies, under preset criteria. This would establish that rebuilding tissue preserves reliable early healing.

milestones.label: Deep skin wounds recover normal structures and strength
milestones.explanation: Wounds through the full skin thickness would have to recover normal layers, structures such as hair follicles, and measured mechanical function. This would distinguish rebuilt skin from a less visible scar.

milestones.label: Joined bowel regains normal structure and resistance to bursting
milestones.explanation: Joined bowel would have to restore its architecture, resist bursting comparably to uninjured bowel and avoid harmful narrowing. This would establish both tissue recovery and a lasting open passage.

milestones.label: The abdominal lining recovers without unwanted attachments
milestones.explanation: Injured abdominal lining would have to restore its surface cell layer and remain free of adhesions when examined beyond 90 days. This would establish surface repair alongside lasting prevention of attachments.

milestones.label: Tendons recover structure, strength and free movement
milestones.explanation: Injured tendons would have to regain organized structure, mechanical performance and smooth movement without restrictive attachments. This would establish recovery of their load-bearing and gliding functions.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce lasting recovery within stated limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce recovery with follow-up long enough to detect late scarring, narrowing or lost function. Stated testing boundaries would define where the treatment works.

uncertain: It remains unknown whether one treatment can rebuild all the intended tissues or whether each needs a different approach.
Which features of fetal healing are necessary or sufficient for controlled repair in adults remains unclear.
Thresholds for adequate early strength, restored architecture, bowel narrowing and tendon recovery still need to be defined.

page.title: Regenerative healing of adult surgical wounds
page.definition: Adult surgical wounds restore the injured tissue’s native architecture and function while maintaining wound closure. Regeneration rebuilds tissue-specific structures; fibrosis replaces them with scar tissue.

goal.need: Foster et al. report adhesions after 50–90% of abdominal operations; these fibrous attachments contribute to bowel obstruction, chronic pain and infertility. Mascharak et al. describe skin scars as having ≤80% of unwounded skin’s strength. Regenerative repair targets the architecture and function lost during scar formation.

statements.body: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
statements.quote: The complete regeneration of injured or diseased human skin remains the ultimate goal and a major challenge of regenerative medicine.
statements.context: The institute’s strategic plan distinguishes tissue regeneration from wound closure with scar formation.

statements.body: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
statements.quote: aim to restore tissue or organ structure and function using tissue engineering and biologics.
statements.context: The regenerative-medicine priority includes skin and tendon and explicitly includes research on healing after surgery.

statements.body: Stanford University-led wound-regeneration developers, Mascharak et al.
statements.quote: regrowth of dermal appendages, reestablishment of normal matrix ultrastructure, and restoration of mechanical robustness.
statements.context: The authors identify these requirements for a successful skin-scar therapy; dermal appendages include hair follicles and sebaceous glands.

completion.title: Controlled human evidence demonstrates regeneration of adult surgical wounds in all four tissues.
completion.criterion: For each listed tissue, controlled clinical evidence in adults demonstrates restoration of native tissue architecture and tissue-specific function after a defined surgical injury, while maintaining wound closure. Structural, functional and healing-safety endpoints distinguish regeneration from reduced fibrosis or fewer adhesions. Different interventions may satisfy different tissue cases. The sources identify no common numerical success margin or follow-up duration; these remain undefined rather than being assigned Atlas values.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; no shared clinical completion test was located for the four tissues.
completion.basis: Searches covered NIAMS strategic plans, FDA wound-product guidance and clinical-development rules, the ACS-affiliated adhesions-development roadmap, and scar-prevention registries. No shared clinical regeneration test for these four tissues was found. NIAMS specifies restoration of structure and function; this Atlas test applies that goal to adult surgical wounds without adding numerical cutoffs.

milestones.title: An adult animal surgical wound regains tissue-specific architecture and function.
milestones.criterion: An adult animal surgical wound recovers tissue-specific structures, matrix organization and function against unwounded and scar-healing controls. Skin: mouse work published on 23 April 2021 reported regenerated appendages and matrix remodeling through postoperative day 90; endpoint-specific animal counts could not be verified. Bowel/peritoneum: the anti-JUN abstract reports reduced adhesions, without establishing regeneration. Fetal skin supplies a developmental precedent. No common numerical cross-tissue threshold was located.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas, generalising the structural and functional skin criterion published by Mascharak et al.; no common animal threshold was located for all four tissues.

milestones.title: Preclinical safety evidence permits a human study of a wound-regeneration drug.
milestones.criterion: For a wound-regeneration drug, pharmacology and toxicology evidence supports the conclusion that the proposed human investigation is reasonably safe. The investigational new drug application (IND) becomes effective 30 days after FDA receipt unless placed on clinical hold, or earlier following FDA notification. The sponsor and investigators must meet the applicable clinical-investigation and human-subject protection requirements. These provisions describe the drug-development pathway.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8) and 312.40.
milestones.threshold_quote: reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations.

milestones.title: An adult receives a wound-regeneration drug in an authorised clinical investigation.
milestones.criterion: At least one adult with a defined surgical wound receives the investigational wound-regeneration drug in an authorised clinical investigation, beginning prospective assessment of exposure, pharmacological effects and adverse effects. FDA defines phase 1 by initial human introduction and studies supporting subsequent controlled investigations. Its typical participant range is descriptive, not a required success threshold.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a), with clinical use governed by 312.40.
milestones.threshold_quote: initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: Controlled human studies show preliminary effectiveness of a wound-regeneration drug.
milestones.criterion: Controlled clinical studies in patients with a defined surgical wound provide preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness for the proposed regenerative indication and characterize common short-term adverse effects. FDA identifies preliminary effectiveness evidence as the prerequisite for phase 3 investigation. It publishes no universal numerical efficacy cutoff. Improvement in scar appearance or adhesion burden supports those narrower indications and does not establish the completion test.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, phase 2 objectives and the prerequisite for phase 3 in 21 CFR 312.21(b)–(c); no tissue-regeneration-specific efficacy threshold is supplied.
milestones.threshold_quote: after preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness of the drug has been obtained

not_found: Controlled adult human evidence satisfying the four-tissue completion test was not located.
The mouse skin study’s supplementary files could not be opened, leaving endpoint-specific animal counts unverified.
The anti-JUN publisher full text was inaccessible; its institutional abstract did not supply animal counts, numerical effects or follow-up.
Primary registry pages for NCT06944249 and NCT07488988 yielded no readable study details.
No adult bowel, peritoneal or tendon result meeting the structural and functional animal criterion could be verified.
